title: SYSK Selects: How Sushi Works
summary: SYSK Selects rerun of the "How Sushi Works" episode. Hosts trace sushi's history from fermented fish preserved in rice in Southeast Asia, through Japanese pickling with sake and rice vinegar, to Edo-era hand-pressed nigiri and its spread to America (California roll, Los Angeles, New York in the 1990s). They cover common sushi ingredients (raw fish, tuna varieties, eel, tamago, avocado), sashimi vs. sushi terminology, wasabi and soy sauce etiquette, sake pairing, sushi chef training, live sushi (ikizukuri), and a step-by-step guide to making sushi rice, nigiri, maki, and hand rolls. The episode ends with a listener mail about rotation plasty.

segments.title: Opening banter and sushi cravings
segments.summary: The hosts open the Selects rerun, joke about craving sushi, and discuss that sushi refers to vinegared rice rather than raw fish, plus the difference between sushi, sashimi, tempura, and hibachi.

segments.title: Origins of sushi: fermented fish
segments.summary: The hosts describe folklore about an osprey nest and the earliest sushi as fish fermented in rice in Southeast Asia, which was later refined in Japan by adding sake and gutting the fish.

segments.title: Edo-era vinegar rice and the birth of nigiri
segments.summary: Rice vinegar sped up preparation, leading to oshi sushi pressed in boxes in Kyoto, and then to Yohei Hanaya's hand-formed nigiri sold from a cart in Edo (Tokyo). The Great Kanto earthquake later moved sushi carts into restaurants.

segments.title: Sushi spreads to America
segments.summary: Sushi grows in popularity in Japan after refrigeration and the postwar economy. It arrives in the US in 1960s Los Angeles with Kawafuku, and the California roll is created in 1973. The hosts say sushi reached New York in the 1990s through Nobu.

segments.title: Sushi ingredients: fish, tuna, eel, and vegetables
segments.summary: The hosts discuss common sushi ingredients, saltwater versus freshwater fish and parasites, freshwater eel, and blue fin tuna prices, including a record sale at the Tokyo Fish Market. They also discuss ethics of tuna farming and live sushi (ikizukuri).

segments.title: Roe, tamago, avocado, and sushi variations
segments.summary: The hosts discuss fish roe, tamago egg sushi, avocado, unusual American toppings, and chirashi bowls. They mention a beef bowl chain and other variations.

segments.title: Eating sushi and wasabi etiquette
segments.summary: The hosts explain traditional etiquette: eating nigiri with hands, dipping fish side lightly in soy sauce, not drowning rice, and wasabi usually placed under the topping. They describe real wasabi versus horseradish and mustard paste, and the sushi chef's social role.

segments.title: Sake pairing and sushi chef training
segments.summary: The hosts discuss sake etiquette, pouring for others, alternatives like green tea and beer, and the training of sushi chefs in Japan and the US, along with discrimination against women chefs. They recommend the documentary Jiro Dreams of Sushi.

segments.title: Making sushi at home
segments.summary: The hosts give a step-by-step guide to choosing sashimi-grade fish, rinsing and cooking sushi rice, seasoning it with rice vinegar, shaping nigiri, rolling maki and hand rolls, and using molds.

segments.title: Sushi facts from The Story of Sushi
segments.summary: The hosts cover facts from Trevor Corson's book: miso soup served at the end of the meal, looser nigiri in Japan, samurai-sword lineage of sushi knives, and the tuna sale figures.

segments.title: Listener mail: rotation plasty
segments.summary: A listener named Kelly writes about rotation plasty, a limb-salvage procedure in which the lower leg is turned backward and the ankle becomes a functional knee. The hosts say they covered it previously, and sign off with contact information.
